output.summary: No interaction requires a change to riluzole 50 mg twice daily; omeprazole may modestly lower riluzole exposure. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for the first 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x ULN. action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles with chronic neurogenic change in the tongue and hand muscles, normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block, and normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No brainstem structural lesion or white matter lesion; corticospinal tract T2/FLAIR hyperintensity is supportive only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs, including brainstem stroke, tumour or demyelination in a patient whose disease began with bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No cervical or thoracic cord compression, cord signal abnormality or mass.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 540 U/L (3.2x ULN); normal blood count, renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function on replacement, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic: thyroid function also checks her levothyroxine replacement.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 76% predicted and SNIP 54 cmH2O reduced, and NIF -48 cmH2O meets an AAN 2009 marker of respiratory insufficiency.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansion and no pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in SOD1, TARDBP, FUS or TBK1.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No interaction requiring a change: levothyroxine none, omeprazole may modestly lower riluzole exposure; transaminases checked before the first dose and on schedule, stop if ALT exceeds 5x ULN.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Omeprazole is a CYP1A2 inducer that may modestly lower riluzole exposure without needing a dose change; levothyroxine does not interact.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
Do not delay the swallowing assessment in a patient who is already choking or coughing on food or fluids.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bulbar weakness (dysarthria, coughing on thin liquids) followed by hand weakness, with upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps reflexes, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs, spastic gait) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar and cervical regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now and discuss NIV: NIF -48 cmH2O meets an AAN 2009 marker of respiratory insufficiency; assess orthopnoea and overnight oximetry or capnography to time NIV, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.

Arrange a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment now (aspiration risk, safe food and fluid consistencies) and a dietetic review with baseline weight, and discuss gastrostomy early, while FVC is above 50% predicted, with voice and communication support given her profession.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, brisk biceps reflexes, bilateral Hoffman and Babinski signs and a spastic gait with lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar and cervical regions, with active denervation also in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles. This is a bulbar-onset ALS phenotype.
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy.
CK 540 U/L (3.2x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 76% predicted and SNIP 54 cmH2O are reduced, and NIF -48 cmH2O already meets an AAN 2009 marker. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).
Bulbar involvement carries a worse prognosis and an aspiration risk; swallowing assessment and early gastrostomy discussion, while FVC is above 50% predicted, are priorities.

findings.finding: Tongue: fibrillations +2, large polyphasic MUPs (chronic denervation/reinnervation), reduced recruitment. Mentalis: fasciculations.
Bilateral FDI, APB: fibrillations +2, positive sharp waves, large MUPs (duration >14ms). Bilateral deltoids: fasciculations +1. Cervical paraspinals C5-C7: fibrillations +1.
Bilateral tibialis anterior: fasciculations. Left gastrocnemius: fibrillations +1.
Median, ulnar, sural: normal amplitude and conduction velocities throughout. No sensory neuropathy.
Median motor (bilateral): CMAP amplitudes reduced (right 3.8 mV, left 3.2 mV; reference >4.5 mV). Normal distal latencies and conduction velocities. No conduction block.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation in bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral muscles, with chronic neurogenic change (large polyphasic motor unit potentials, reduced recruitment) in the tongue and hand muscles and fasciculation potentials in the mentalis, deltoids and tibialis anterior. 2. Reduced median CMAP amplitudes bilaterally with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block. 3. Normal sensory conduction studies. Findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells, consistent with a motor neuron disease.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive speech changes and bilateral hand weakness over 11 months

social_history.occupation: Retired professional soprano, now voice coach

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. V is a 64-year-old retired professional soprano and current voice coach who presents with an 11-month history of progressive dysarthria, voice changes, and bilateral hand weakness. As a professional voice user, she first noticed subtle changes in her vocal quality approximately 11 months ago, which she initially attributed to vocal fatigue or aging. Over the ensuing months, her speech became increasingly nasal and hypophonic, and she began to have difficulty sustaining high notes during her coaching sessions. She subsequently noticed progressive weakness in both hands, finding it increasingly difficult to demonstrate piano playing technique and to button her shirt. Approximately 6 months ago, her students began commenting on visible muscle twitching in her arms during lessons. Her husband noticed her tongue fasciculating approximately 4 months ago. She has no history of botulinum toxin injections to the vocal cords. Her levothyroxine dose has been stable for 3 years with consistent normal TSH. She has no dysphagia to solids but reports occasional coughing with thin liquids. She denies any cognitive changes. Her progression has been relentless and she reports marked functional decline over the past 6 months compared to her initial presentation.

neurological_exam.additional: Voice changes are particularly distressing to her as a voice professional.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Tongue atrophy bilateral, visible fasciculations at rest. Dysarthria — nasal quality, hypophonic. Jaw jerk brisk. Palatal elevation asymmetric (right reduced).
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Emotional about changes to her voice.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral hand intrinsic weakness with wasting. Right shoulder abduction 4/5. Fasciculations visible in bilateral deltoids, triceps, and calves.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 3+ bilaterally. Hoffmans bilateral. Bilateral Babinski positive.
